Briefly stated, the facts giving rise to the present appeal are that the plaintiffs filed a Civil Suit before the learned .

Trial Court seeking a mandatory injunction directing the defendants to initiate the acquisition proceedings to acquire the land bearing Khata/Khatauni No. 29/45 min, Khasra No. 572/1, 5 Biswa,
situated in Mauza Raher, Pargana Pashgaon, Tehsil Kandaghat, District Solan, H.P. (hereinafter referred to the 'suit land').
It was asserted that the plaintiffs are owners of the suit land.

The defendants constructed a bridge connecting Mauza Raher with Mauza Karganoo, Tehsil Rajgarh,
District Sirmour, H.P.
Defendants occupied the suit land for the construction of the bridge without consent of the plaintiffs and payment of any compensation as per law.

The defendants assured the plaintiffs to pay the compensation as per the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, but no steps were taken to acquire the land and to pay the compensation to the plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs issued a notice to the defendants asking them to initiate the proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act but the defendants did not respond.
Hence, the suit was filed seeking relief mentioned above.

and cause of action, the plaintiffs being estopped from filing the present suit, by their acts and conduct, the suit being barred by limitation, the plaintiffs having not come to the Court with clean hands and the suit not being properly valued for Court fees.

8. Being aggrieved from the judgment and decree passed by the learned Trial Court, the defendants filed an appeal, which was decided by the learned District Judge, Solan, H.P. (Learned First Appellate Court).
Learned First Appellate Court held that the ownership of the suit land was not disputed.
It was also not disputed that the construction of the bridge was raised by the defendants over the suit land.
There was no evidence of the consent of the plaintiffs and merely because the plaintiffs had not objected, their right would not be taken away.
The State has to act impartially and without any favour to any person.
It cannot utilize the land of the private persons without payment of the compensation.
Hence, the judgment and decree passed by the learned Trial Court were set aside and directions were issued to acquire the land as per law.

1) Whether on account of misappreciation of the pleadings and misreading of the oral as well as documentary evidence available on record, the findings recorded by the learned lower appellate Court are erroneous and as such the judgment and decree impugned in the main appeal being perverse and vitiated is not legally sustainable?

This amounts to the admission of the defendants that the bridge was constructed on the suit land.
Hence, both the learned Courts below had rightly held that the plaintiffs are owners of the suit land and the bridge was constructed on the suit land.
16. The defendants asserted in their written statement that the construction was raised with the consent of the plaintiffs.

Before proceeding to deal with the issue of the legitimacy of the land acquisition proceeding, it would be .
appropriate to set out the international legal framework on compulsory land acquisition.

The right to self- determination is enshrined within the Charter of the United Nations, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights ("ICESCR") and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights ("ICCPR"), amongst other instruments which is defined as the right of all people to freely dispose of their natural wealth and resources, and that no person may be deprived of its own means of subsistence.

sentences.text: Article 17 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that, "Everyone has the right to own property alone as well as in association with others.

Self- determination also includes an obligation for States to refrain from any forcible actions that deprive people of enjoying such rights.

The concept of Free, Prior and Informed Consent ("FPIC") within international development law is most clearly stated in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in Articles 10, 11, 19, 28 and 29 which prescribe situations in which FPIC must be obtained before granting compensation, taking of indigenous property, etc.

Development experts have recognised that FPIC is not only important for indigenous people but can also be used as a positive approach to involve local communities in decision-making about any proposed development.

Engaging them in such processes fosters a greater sense of ownership and engagement and, moreover, helps safeguard their right to development as a basic human rights principle [ Sambhav Shrivastava et al.,

The outcome of the extensive study of around 1269 judgments of the Supreme Court of India between 1950 to 2016 on the legal trajectory of land acquisition cases in India lead to the following comments:
"The process of land acquisition in India has been the source of increasing political and legal contestation for almost two hundred years.
This stems from the inherently coercive nature of the process, which creates a severe imbalance in power between the State and land losers.

Our review of the Supreme Court litigation since the time India became a constitutional republic in 1950 shows that while much of this imbalance was created within the very text of the Land Acquisition Act, a considerable part of it could also be attributed to executive non-compliance with the rule of law.
The result was a situation of great inequity for the land losers."
